title: Saint Thomas Christian communities on the Malabar Coast
summary: Christians of Kerala trace their origin to the apostle Thomas, said by tradition to have reached south India in 52 CE; this is belief, not documented history. The earliest outside evidence is later: a 4th-century Persian bishop's title, and Cosmas Indicopleustes noting a church at Malabar and Persian-appointed clergy in the early 6th century.

uncertainty.note: The 52 CE date is a pious tradition and cannot be confirmed; the record is anchored on it only because that is how the tradition is dated.

as_recorded.value: St. Thomas, according to tradition, arrived in South India in 52
c. 530-535: Christian community at Male (Malabar); bishop at Caliana
c. 325: John the Persian signed as presiding over churches in Persia and Great India

when.display: Tradition: 52 CE (legendary); earliest evidence 4th–6th century CE

where.historical_name: Malabar Coast of southwestern India (Muziris–Cranganore area), a region of Red Sea trade

importance.justification: One of the oldest Christian communities outside the Roman and Persian worlds, with a long-lived Syriac-linked church in India.

sources.title: Thomas Christians
sources.publisher: Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage (Beth Mardutho)

reviewer_note: Tradition (Thomas arrives 52) and earliest evidence (4th–6th century) are kept apart. Pin at Kodungallur is the Cranganore of the later community tradition; no opened source locates the supposed landing, so uncertainty is wide. GEDSH reads the date as "52" without stating CE; the CE reading is inferred. The Kalyan/Quilon identification of Cosmas's Caliana is disputed.
